signals.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
signals.content: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
Computer-use agents are constrained by the interfaces humans provide. An agent may manually fill a spreadsheet cell‑by‑cell when a single line of code would suffice, or dump an entire 2,000‑line file to locate a function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to apply them are handcrafted, limiting scalability as new applications, workflows, and models emerge. We propose that interface design itself become an agent capability. Agent S4 is an autonomous computer‑use scientist that constructs Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta‑agent observes task agents’ trajectories on synthetic training tasks—without explicit success labels—and iteratively builds and revises a repository of interfaces and usage heuristics. Population‑based evolution then selects repositories that perform best on unseen validation tasks, favoring generalizable improvements. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4 (Qwen3.8‑27B) with the evolved repository achieves a 21.3 % binary score, 3.8× the same model with static interfaces, surpassing GPT‑5.5 (13.0 %) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6 %) at roughly 4.3 % and 1.5 % of their costs. On ScienceBoard, success rises from 41.4 % to 58.6 % with the same model. These findings indicate that functional interfaces can be evolved from experience, enabling autonomous interface design for future AI agents.

العنوان: واجهات الوكلاء المتطورة
تقتصر قدرة الوكلاء الذين يستخدمون الحاسوب على الواجهات التي يزوّدها البشر. قد يملأ الوكيل جدولًا خليةً بخليةً يدويًا بينما يكفي سطر برمجي واحد، أو يطبع ملفًا مكوّنًا من 2000 سطر للبحث عن دالة واحدة. كل من الواجهات ومعرفة متى تُستَخدم تُصنع يدويًا، ما يمنعها من مواكبة التطبيقات وسير العمل والنماذج الجديدة. نقترح أن يصبح تصميم الواجهة قدرةً للوكيل نفسه. يقدم Agent S4 عالمًا ذاتيًا لاستخدام الحاسوب يبني "واجهات الوكلاء المتطورة" من خبرة المهام. يراقب وكيل ميتا مسارات وكلاء المهام على مهام تدريب اصطناعية دون علامات نجاح، ويُنشئ ويُحدّث مستودعًا للواجهات ومعارف الاستخدام. ثم تختار عملية تطور سكانية المستودعات التي تحقق أفضل أداء على مهام تحقق غير مرئية للميتّا، مفضلةً التغييرات القابلة للتعميم. على OSWorld V2، يحقق Agent S4 (Qwen3.8‑27B) مع المستودع المتطور درجة 21.3٪، أي 3.8× للنموذج نفسه بواجهات ثابتة، متفوقًا على GPT‑5.5 (13.0٪) وClaude Opus 4.8 (20.6٪) بتكلفة تقارب 4.3٪ و1.5٪ من تكلفتهما. على ScienceBoard ارتفع معدل النجاح من 41.4٪ إلى 58.6٪ مع نفس النموذج. تشير هذه النتائج إلى إمكانية تطور واجهات مفيدة من الخبرة، مما يمكّن التصميم الذاتي للواجهات في الوكلاء المستقبلية.

signals.content: 🚨MORE MAVEN🚨 Marine Corps moves to expand Maven Smart System account access across its enterprise The Marine Corps has instructed organizations across all of its echelons to provide authorized personnel with their own Maven Smart System accounts on the applicable networks that they are permitted to access. This significant expansion of enterprise licensing for Palantir’s AI-powered software platform went into effect Oct. 1, according to an administrative message posted online Tuesday. “Other guidance such as an updated MSS Implementation Plan will be published separately,” officials wrote. With roots that trace back over the last decade to Project Maven, MSS is now evolving into the central cornerstone of the U.S. military’s complex plan to consolidate sprawling and fragmented command-and-control assets into a unified operating picture that can speed up commanders’ decision-making. The platform captures and fuses vast streams of intelligence and other data — including computer vision and object detection from drone videos, satellite imagery, troop records, logistics, and supply chain status — to support real-world combat operations. In the administrative message released this week, MSS is described as a government-owned, contractor-operated, commercial software platform containing Defense Department-owned data and interfaces “that enable integration of strategic, operational, and tactical data to support all Joint functions.” A source familiar with the work who requested anonymity to speak about the expansion told DefenseScoop that it’s significant in that it will grant the Marine Corps “unfettered access to MSS unclassified secret and top secret” capabilities, which they said are envisioned to introduce unprecedented interoperability and true situational awareness across any connected battlespace that the service operates in. MSS has been scaling rapidly across the Defense Department and military services under the second Trump administration. Last year, DOD raised its contract ceiling with Palantir for the technology to nearly $1.3 billion through 2029. Senior officials indicated that the move was necessary to meet “growing demand.” The Marine Corps has simultaneously been taking major steps to integrate and adopt the AI platform and associated C2 capabilities. Its specialized Task Force Maven and Project Dynamis teams lead efforts to operationalize MSS. n August, the Corps hosted the Maven Smart System Summit in Virginia, where government and military officials discussed service-wide integration pursuits, including in edge and tactical environments. “This enterprise licensing provides all assigned and attached personnel at any echelon within the specified commands the ability to gain MSS accounts within those domains they have authorized access,” the new administrative message states. The message refers to the “Covered units” and their subordinate entities listed in prior MSS integration guidance published by the service last year — with the addition of Marine Forces Reserve Command. “Fleet Marine Force (FMF) Headquarters as well as Functional and Geographic Marine Forces Command (MARFOR) Headquarters are provided with accounts through their associated Combatant Command Headquarters,” per the latest directive. Among its instructions to deliver the system licenses, the Corps’ commands are told to designate an MSS implementation lead and determine their counterparts at higher and subordinate echelons. “Flag-level commands are requested to identify their designated MSS implementation lead/Office of Primary Responsibility (OPR) to Project Dynamis/TF Maven for on-going coordination and support,” officials wrote. Spokespersons from the Pentagon, Palantir and the Marine Corps did not immediately answer questions from DefenseScoop regarding what prompted the message, the dollar value of the associated contract and other topics.

signals.title: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics
signals.content: Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability, an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, it bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building on this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We show conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. We also specify an open-source validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper on exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking.

A specialized LLM engine then processes the pruned subgraph to produce targeted, code-level root cause analyses and actionable remediation strategies, effectively filtering ambient telemetry noise and accelerating incident response.

signals.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
signals.content: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

In a case study on 14 asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw identified defect structures, quantified deformation modes, and showed that secondary GB misfit dislocations significantly affect shear strength. Follow‑up calculations linked unusually high shear resistance to metastable boundary configurations, highlighting the framework’s ability to uncover mechanistic insights in complex, under‑explored interfaces.

signals.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
signals.content: Large Language Model (LLM) agents can handle increasingly complex tasks, navigating long trajectories of observations and actions. As these trajectories grow, key-value (KV) cache I/O and storage become the dominant cost. Trajectories can also exceed the LLM's maximum context length, requiring control over active cache growth. Prior work uses context engineering to reduce cache size by trimming or summarizing history. However, modifying the trajectory prefix invalidates subsequent cached states and triggers costly re-prefilling of retained context. Task accuracy can also suffer when too little context is retained to limit re-prefill costs. We propose cache engineering as a new scheme. It allows agents to directly control their active KV cache without modifying the trajectory or re-prefilling retained context. Specifically, agents can proactively use drop to exclude selected cache from future attention and repos to adjust retained keys' position encodings. We formalize these cache operations and identify history dependence as a serving challenge: identical token sequences can yield different cache states under different cache operation sequences, making prefix matching insufficient for correct cache reuse. Thus, we co-design the AKV serving engine. It provides a stateless interface compatible with existing serving APIs, while internally managing stateful cache reuse, eviction, and restoration. Experiments show that a tool-response rolling-drop cache policy improves average benchmark scores by 1.7 points and reduces average cost by 27.7%, compared with conventional threshold-triggered summarization. With AKV, it achieves up to 1.2x the output throughput and a 1.5x speedup in P95 request latency. Recursive self-improvement of cache policies further reduces cost by 7.1% over expert design. Our code is at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV.

signals.brief_en: Cache Engineering for Agents: LLM agents face rising KV‑cache I/O and storage costs as task trajectories lengthen, often exceeding context windows. Traditional context engineering trims or summarizes history but invalidates cached states, forcing costly re‑prefill and risking accuracy loss. The proposed cache engineering scheme lets agents directly manage the active KV cache: ‘drop’ excludes selected entries from future attention, and ‘repos’ shifts retained keys’ position encodings. Because identical token sequences can produce different cache states depending on operation order, simple prefix matching fails; thus a co‑designed AKV serving engine offers a stateless API while internally handling stateful cache reuse, eviction, and restoration. Experiments show that a rolling‑drop policy for tool responses reduces average re‑prefill overhead while preserving task performance.

signals.title: InterWebCoder: Learning Interactive Webpage Generation from Executable Tests via Reinforcement Learning
signals.content: Interactive webpages underpin modern applications, but reproducing both their visual appearance and multi-step behavior remains challenging for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Scalable training data must capture user actions, state transitions, and expected outcomes, while real-world webpage code is often entangled with irrelevant scripts and external dependencies. Moreover, existing GUI-agent-based verification provides slow and potentially unstable functional feedback. To address these challenges, we propose InterWebCoder, an efficient framework for interactive webpage code generation. InterWebCoder introduces a Test-Specification-Guided and Execution-Verified Data Synthesis pipeline that records real-world interaction trajectories and synthesizes self-contained webpage code with executable test scripts. A failureattributed repair mechanism uses runtime evidence to locate and iteratively fix errors in either the webpage code or test script. We then combine test-ID-weighted supervised fine-tuning with group-relative policy optimization, directly optimizing functional correctness and visual fidelity using test pass rates and state-level visual similarity. This replaces costly GUI-agent verification with fast, reproducible executable feedback. Our pipeline produces 1,736 verified samples from 2,058 tasks, achieving an 84.35% synthesis success rate. On IWR-Bench and Vision2Web, InterWebCoder achieves final scores of 48.54 and 48.42 with a 9B backbone, outperforming 30B-level models and Gemini-3.7-Flash while remaining competitive with Claude-Sonnet-5. It reduces reward-computation latency by over 97%, eliminates external MLLM verification costs, and accelerates end-to-end training by up to 1.4x.

signals.brief_en: InterWebCoder is a framework for generating interactive web pages from executable tests using reinforcement learning. It captures real user interaction trajectories, synthesizes self‑contained page code with test scripts, and employs a failure‑attributed repair loop to fix code or test errors. Training combines test‑ID‑weighted supervised fine‑tuning with group‑relative policy optimization, directly optimizing functional correctness and visual fidelity via test pass rates and visual similarity metrics. The pipeline produced 1,736 verified samples from 2,058 tasks, achieving an 84.35% synthesis success rate and scoring 48.54 on IWR‑Bench and 48.42 on Vision2Web with a 9B model, surpassing comparable baselines.

signals.title: The Token-Energy Law of LLM Decode: Active Bytes and Realized Time Account for Joules per Token
signals.content: Energy-efficient deployment of large language models requires understanding how model architecture, hardware, and serving settings shape energy per generated token. We introduce the Token-Energy Law, a compact, interpretable model of GPU-board energy per output token for dense, full-history decoding. It relates token energy to two core dimensions: active bytes and realized decode time. Active bytes describe logical byte demand per output, separating dense weights shared within a decode iteration from private key--value (KV) histories read and updated for each request. Realized decode time is the elapsed decode duration divided by the number of output tokens produced. We combine the two byte coordinates and time in a common affine form, with coefficients calibrated for each model and hardware/runtime configuration. This formulation explains how batching amortizes shared-weight work, longer attended histories increase private KV demand, and throughput determines the time-associated cost per output. Our experiments cover three models under BF16 decoding on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, including two-GPU tensor parallelism on Hopper. Using fixed coefficients and observed decode time, held-out condition-mean energy estimates differ from measurements by at most 3.73%.

signals.brief_en: The Token‑Energy Law of LLM Decode: Active Bytes and Realized Time Account for Joules per Token – Energy‑efficient LLM serving hinges on quantifying how architecture, hardware and serving parameters translate into joules per generated token. The law models GPU‑board energy for dense, full‑history decoding as an affine function of two variables: (1) active bytes, the logical byte demand per output token, split into shared dense‑weight bytes (common to all requests in a decode step) and private key‑value (KV) bytes (read/updated per request’s attention history); (2) realized decode time, the elapsed decode duration divided by the number of output tokens. Model‑specific coefficients are calibrated for each GPU (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell) and runtime setting (BF16, tensor‑parallelism). The formulation captures three effects: batching amortizes shared‑weight work, longer KV histories raise private byte demand, and higher throughput reduces the time‑associated energy per token. Experiments on three BF16 models across Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (including two‑GPU tensor parallelism) show mean prediction errors ≤ 3.73 % versus measured energy, confirming the law’s practical accuracy for strategic deployment planning.
signals.brief_ar: قانون طاقة الرموز في فك تشفير نماذج اللغة الكبيرة: البايتات النشطة والوقت المحقق يحسبان الجول لكل رمز – تحقيق كفاءة الطاقة في تشغيل نماذج اللغة الكبيرة يتطلب قياس كيفية تحويل بنية النموذج، العتاد وإعدادات الخدمة إلى استهلاك جول لكل رمز مُنتج. يصف القانون طاقة لوحة الـ GPU أثناء فك تشفير كامل التاريخ بكثافة كدالة خطية (affine) تعتمد على متغيرين أساسيين: (1) البايتات النشطة، أي الطلب البايتاتي المنطقي لكل رمز، مقسَّم إلى بايتات الأوزان الكثيفة المشتركة بين جميع الطلبات في خطوة فك التشفير، و بايتات المفتاح‑القيمة (KV) الخاصة التي تُقرأ وتُحدَّث حسب تاريخ الانتباه لكل طلب؛ (2) الوقت المحقق، وهو مدة فك التشفير مقسومة على عدد الرموز المُنتجة. تُضبط معاملات النموذج حسب كل GPU (مثل NVIDIA Hopper أو Blackwell) وإعدادات التنفيذ (BF16، التوازي على عدة وحدات). يوضح النموذج ثلاثة تأثيرات: تجميع الطلبات يقلل من تكلفة الأوزان المشتركة، إطالة تاريخ KV يزيد الطلب الخاص على البايتات، وزيادة الإنتاجية تخفض تكلفة الطاقة المرتبطة بالوقت لكل رمز. تجارب على ثلاثة نماذج BF16 على GPUs Hopper و Blackwell (بما فيها التوازي على وحدتين) أظهرت أخطاء تنبؤية بمتوسط ≤ 3.73 % مقارنةً بالقياسات الفعلية، ما يؤكد موثوقية القانون لتخطيط النشر الاستراتيجي.
